passage:
Monday morning, Keerthana looked at her week: a pair of assignments, the lab record, and a club event on Saturday. She wrote each deadline and its marks next to it. The club event counted for nothing towards grades and came last, so she dropped it from her list and told Ganga she could not run it.

On Sunday evening she opened the calendar and blocked in her lectures, study hours, lunches, gym and bedtime. Between them she left empty half-hours for surprises, and a surprise did come: the lab teacher asked for a redo.

Across the hostel, Anand said "two hours" about a report and opened it at ten that night. At six in the morning he was still typing, with a cold cup of tea beside him. The next week he said "two hours" again, and again he lost the night.

After the third time, he looked back at his old attempts: everything had taken about double. He made every guess half as long again and started a day earlier. When the next deadline came, Anand was already done, and the panic simply did not arrive.

qa.q: What did Keerthana drop from her list?
qa.a: She dropped the club event.

qa.q: How did Keerthana plan her week differently from Anand, and why did hers hold together?
qa.a: Keerthana ranked tasks by deadline and marks and left empty half-hours for surprises, so the lab redo fitted in, while Anand kept saying two hours and starting late until he made every guess half as long again.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling at six in the morning?
qa.a: Exhausted and probably frustrated, still typing with a cold cup of tea beside him.

qa.q: What could Anand do to keep the habit going?
qa.a: Anand could keep making his guesses half as long again and check them against how long tasks really took.

grounding: Four approaches to a heavy semester: ranking by deadline and marks, a weekly time-block schedule, underestimating task length, and adding a buffer after overruns.

passage:
Rekha wrote it on a sticky note above the bathroom mirror: once the toothbrush goes down, I go for a twenty-minute walk. She no longer had to decide anything each morning; the toothbrush was the signal.

Manoj stretched for just ten minutes and jogged slowly to the corner and back. On bad days, the stretching alone counted. Each week he added a few minutes, and by March his jog reached the park.

Jeevan, motivated on the first of January, paid for a full year at a gym and planned hard workouts every day. Then a cold and a crowded work week broke his streak. He looked at the calendar, felt like a failure, and never went back.

In April Manoj missed a week. He did not drop the plan; he wrote down what had happened. The evening sessions were the ones that failed, when he was tired and hungry. He moved everything to mornings, and set one rule: never miss twice in a row.

qa.q: What was Rekha's signal to start walking?
qa.a: Her signal was putting down the toothbrush.

qa.q: How did Jeevan's plan differ from Manoj's, and what happened when each hit a bad week?
qa.a: Jeevan planned hard daily workouts and dropped everything after one broken streak, while Manoj started small, treated the missed week as information, moved sessions to mornings and set a rule never to miss twice.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling after the streak broke?
qa.a: Like a failure, which made him give up completely.

qa.q: What could Jeevan try instead?
qa.a: Jeevan could start with a small daily walk and treat a missed day as something to learn from.

grounding: Four approaches to a fitness habit: a fixed cue, a tiny start, an all-or-nothing plan, and adjusting after a missed week.

passage:
Pankaj counted the weeks to the exam on his fingers, then took away the weeks for going over old topics and mock tests. What remained, divided by the syllabus blocks, gave him a handful of days per block, far too few. Something had to be cut. He laid out five years of past papers and saw that two topics carried most of the marks, while three were asked once in a while. He started with the big ones and left the rare ones for last.

Lokesh, in the same coaching centre, joined eleven chat groups, downloaded dozens of PDFs and changed teachers twice in a month. He felt busy all day. When Pankaj asked which book he had finished, Lokesh scratched his head. None.

Pranav studied late every night for two weeks, and his mock scores fell. He looked at the dates and saw that the dips followed the sleepless stretches. He set fixed sleep hours, a short walk each evening and one free evening a week. Three weeks later his answers were more accurate.

qa.q: How many chat groups did Lokesh join?
qa.a: Lokesh joined eleven chat groups.

qa.q: How did Pankaj's approach to the syllabus differ from Lokesh's?
qa.a: Pankaj counted his time and used past papers to start with the topics carrying most of the marks, while Lokesh collected groups, PDFs and teachers and finished no book.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when asked which book he had finished?
qa.a: Embarrassed and a little uneasy, shown by scratching his head.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do next?
qa.a: Lokesh could pick one book and one teacher, finish it chapter by chapter, and use past papers to see what matters.

grounding: Four approaches to preparing for a competitive exam: working backward, prioritising by marks, collecting resources instead of studying, and planning around slumps.

passage:
At the park on Saturday, Uma stood near the swings and watched a boy walk up to a group of children and say, "Can I play too?" The children shuffled over and made room. Uma noticed.

Come Sunday, at the sandpit, Uma walked up to two girls with buckets, smiled, and said, "Can I play too?" One of them handed her a spade.

Salma had a new bicycle with a bell, and she wanted Aman to play tag. She said, "You can have the first turn on my bicycle if you play tag after." Aman rode three times round the path, rang the bell, and then ran to tag her.

Charu had a game of her own in mind. She planted her hands on her hips and told Meera, "You have to play my game or I won't be your friend." Meera looked at her, hugged her doll and walked away to the slide. Charu stood alone in the sand, holding her stick.

qa.q: What did Uma say at the sandpit?
qa.a: Uma said, "Can I play too?"

qa.q: How did Salma's way of getting Aman to play differ from Charu's way with Meera, and what happened?
qa.a: Salma offered the first turn on her bicycle in exchange for tag, and Aman joined in, while Charu demanded that Meera play her game or lose her as a friend, and Meera walked away.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she stood alone in the sand?
qa.a: Sad and left out, though she probably did not understand why Meera left.

qa.q: What could Charu try next time?
qa.a: Charu could ask Meera what she would like to play, or offer her a turn at something.

grounding: Three approaches to getting a friend to play: copying a peer's words, trading a turn for play, and bossing.

The family decided on Agra for the October break. Chinmay made a table with three columns: train, bus, car. The train was cheaper and safer for the night hours; the car could stop anywhere. "Train," he told his parents, and they agreed.

Then he wrote a wish list of six places to see in two days: the fort, a museum, the garden, a water park, the market and the old mosque. His father unrolled the map, pointed to the clock on the wall and said, "Show me how you get from here to there." Chinmay drew lines, counted the travel hours, and slowly crossed off three.

Pallavi made a checklist with their mother, Alka: tickets to book, clothes to pack, snacks and lunch for the train. Every night in the week before, they ticked one line.

At the final planning talk, their father said the family could spend ten thousand rupees. Pallavi added up the entry fees and crossed out the water park. The fort and the museum stayed, and on the last day the whole family said those had been the best part.

qa.q: How many places did Chinmay first put on his wish list?
qa.a: He put six places on his wish list.

qa.q: How did Chinmay's wish list differ from Pallavi's final plan, and what changed each?
qa.a: Chinmay's six places in two days did not fit the travel time until his father showed the map and clock, while Pallavi crossed out the water park to match the ten thousand rupees and kept the fort and the museum.

qa.q: What might Chinmay be feeling as he crosses off three places?
qa.a: Disappointed but accepting, since he drew the lines and counted the hours himself.

qa.q: What could the family do to enjoy the trip?
qa.a: They could keep a little time free and choose the places everyone cares about most.

grounding: Four approaches to planning a family trip: a task checklist, comparing travel options, an unlimited wish list, and adjusting to the budget.

passage:
Swati sat in her high chair with an empty katori. She could not say much, but she tapped the bowl on the tray, looked at her mother Usha and said, "Aur." Usha smiled and filled the bowl again with dal-rice, and Swati patted the tray and got busy with her spoon.

In another kitchen, Varun was hungry too. He tugged at the cupboard where the biscuits lived. It stayed shut. He walked to the fridge and pulled the handle. Nothing. He pointed at the counter and said, "Bi." His father followed his finger and brought a banana.

Varun shoved it away and cried, his face scrunched, his hands out for a biscuit. His father said, "Banana, or wait for dinner." Varun cried harder. Then he sniffled, looked at the banana on the tray, picked it up and took a bite. He chewed slowly, and the crying stopped.

qa.q: What did Swati say while tapping the katori?
qa.a: Swati said, "Aur."

qa.q: How did Swati's way of asking for food differ from Varun's first attempts, and what did each get?
qa.a: Swati handed her mother the empty bowl and got more food at once, while Varun tried the cupboard, the fridge and pointing, and got a banana rather than the biscuit he wanted.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he shoved the banana away?
qa.a: Disappointed and frustrated, because he wanted a biscuit and not a banana.

qa.q: How could Varun's father help?
qa.a: His father could name the choices, say the biscuit is for later, and let Varun pick between the banana and something else.

grounding: Four toddler ways of getting food when hungry: using the caregiver as a tool, trial and error, frustration at a mismatch, and accepting an alternative.
